triage.name: Sore Throat
triage.reason: Very common presentation (pharyngitis) with clear diagnostic reasoning around streptococcal versus viral causes; reachable by history and exam.

demographics: One of the most common reasons for outpatient visits
Peaks in school-age children and young adults
More common in winter and early spring

risk_factors.text: Close contact with someone who has a sore throat or strep throat
Age 5–15 years (highest risk for group A streptococcal pharyngitis)
Crowded settings such as schools, day care, college dormitories or military barracks
Tobacco smoke exposure, including secondhand smoke

social_history: Recent travel or new sexual partner (consider gonococcal pharyngitis)
exposures: Sick contacts with sore throat, cold or flu
Recent upper respiratory infection in the household
Exposure to tobacco smoke or other irritants

chief_complaints.text: My throat feels scratchy and raw

hpi.duration: Usually 3–7 days; may last up to 10 days with viral causes
hpi.progression: Often starts with scratchiness or dryness, then becomes a constant soreness that is worst with swallowing; may improve after 2–3 days or worsen if bacterial
hpi.location: Throat, often worse on one or both sides; may radiate to the ears
hpi.quality: Scratchy, raw, burning or sharp pain
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; severe enough to make swallowing uncomfortable but usually not preventing fluids
hpi.timing: Constant, worse with swallowing; may be worse in the morning
pertinent_negatives: Drooling or inability to swallow saliva
One-sided severe swelling of the throat

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not complain of sore throat; they present with fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting or abdominal pain. Streptococcal pharyngitis is most common in ages 5–15.
May have milder symptoms and lower fever, but higher risk of complications such as dehydration or epiglottitis; sore throat may be the only sign of a serious infection.
Higher risk of severe or unusual infections (e.g., Candida, herpes, bacterial) and may lack classic inflammatory signs; symptoms can be prolonged and atypical.

Sore throat is usually viral and self-limited; however, group A streptococcal infection can be more severe and requires prompt treatment to prevent complications. Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy may be mistaken for swallowing difficulty.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort with swallowing or speaking, otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, muffled or 'hot potato' voice, drooling, sitting upright and leaning forward
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, stridor, unable to swallow saliva, tripod positioning, respiratory distress

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not distinguish viral from bacterial pharyngitis; leukocytosis with neutrophilia is more typical of group A streptococcal infection or a deep neck infection.
Lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes suggests viral causes such as Epstein-Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis).
Supports inflammation but does not separate viral from bacterial pharyngitis.
Not routinely needed; a low value argues against bacterial infection.
Negative. Ordered in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or antibiotics.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected epiglottitis when the airway is stable and the patient can cooperate

findings.text: Normal study does not exclude epiglottitis

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected deep neck infection, peritonsillar or retropharyngeal abscess, or airway compromise

findings.text: Peritonsillar fluid collection with rim enhancement
Retropharyngeal or parapharyngeal fluid collection or abscess
Asymmetric soft tissue swelling and fat stranding

imaging.preferred_when: Children or pregnancy when a deep neck collection is suspected and CT is not desirable

initial.test: Rapid antigen detection test for group A streptococcus
initial.why: Fast, specific test for group A streptococcal pharyngitis when clinical features suggest it
Confirms group A streptococcus when the rapid antigen test is negative in a child or adolescent
initial.only_if: rapid antigen test is negative and the patient is a child or adolescent

initial.test: Infectious mononucleosis test (heterophile antibody or EBV serology)
initial.why: Consider when there is marked lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, prolonged symptoms or atypical lymphocytes
Supports inflammation or suggests a viral cause with atypical lymphocytes
initial.only_if: systemic symptoms, severe illness or suspected mononucleosis

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before antibiotics or imaging

confirmatory.why: Confirms a deep neck space infection or abscess when suspected
confirmatory.only_if: severe pain, trismus, muffled voice, drooling, asymmetric swelling or airway concern

supporting.why: Adds evidence of inflammation but does not distinguish viral from bacterial causes
supporting.only_if: Adds evidence of inflammation but does not distinguish viral from bacterial causes

supporting.why: May show an enlarged epiglottis when epiglottitis is suspected and the airway is stable
supporting.only_if: epiglottitis is suspected and the patient is stable

not_indicated.why: Not needed for typical uncomplicated sore throat; does not reliably separate viral from bacterial causes
Not routine; clinical features and a rapid strep test are more useful
Not indicated unless pneumonia is suspected
not_indicated.only_if: pneumonia is suspected (abnormal vitals or lung exam)
a deep neck infection or abscess is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not indicated for typical sore throat

not_indicated.test: Infectious mononucleosis test (heterophile antibody or EBV serology)
not_indicated.why: Not routine for every sore throat

decision_points: Use a rapid antigen detection test for group A streptococcus when clinical features suggest streptococcal pharyngitis; back it up with a throat culture in children and adolescents if negative.
Do not test or treat for group A streptococcus when viral features such as cough, runny nose, hoarseness or oral ulcers are prominent.
Consider epiglottitis or a deep neck infection when there is drooling, muffled voice, trismus, severe one-sided pain or respiratory distress; keep the airway safe and involve anesthesia or ENT early.
Pregnancy test before antibiotics or CT in anyone who could be pregnant.
Avoid amoxicillin or ampicillin when mononucleosis is suspected because of the risk of a rash.

criteria.name: Centor criteria (modified McIsaac)
criteria.summary: Clinical prediction of group A streptococcal pharyngitis using tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, fever history and absence of cough, with age adjustment; guides whether to test rather than confirming the diagnosis.

differential.name: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis
differential.why_considered: The most important bacterial cause of sore throat and the main reason to test and treat; presents with sore throat, fever and tender neck nodes.
differential.trigger: Sore throat with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, and no cough

history: Absence of cough and runny nose
Age 5–15 years or close contact with strep throat
exam: Tender, enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes
labs: Positive rapid antigen detection test for group A streptococcus

differential.name: Viral pharyngitis (common cold)
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of sore throat overall; viral features are usually prominent.

labs: Negative rapid antigen detection test and throat culture
Normal or mildly elevated white count

differential.name: Infectious mononucleosis
differential.why_considered: Causes severe sore throat with marked lymphadenopathy and can be mistaken for streptococcal pharyngitis; important because of splenic rupture risk and the amoxicillin rash.
differential.trigger: Severe sore throat with marked posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fatigue and prolonged symptoms in an adolescent or young adult

history: Prolonged fatigue and malaise for a week or more
Severe sore throat that does not improve
exam: Tonsillar exudate that can be marked
labs: Positive heterophile antibody test or EBV serology

differential.name: Epiglottitis
differential.why_considered: A life-threatening cause of sore throat and airway obstruction that can be mistaken for ordinary pharyngitis early on.
differential.trigger: Drooling, muffled 'hot potato' voice, severe pain with inability to swallow saliva, or respiratory distress

history: Severe pain with swallowing, unable to swallow saliva
exam: Tripod positioning, sitting upright and leaning forward
labs: Blood cultures may grow the causative organism
imaging: Lateral neck x-ray showing thumb sign (enlarged rounded epiglottis) and thickened aryepiglottic folds
Direct visualization by an experienced clinician showing a cherry-red, swollen epiglottis

differential.name: Peritonsillar abscess
differential.why_considered: A deep neck infection that begins as tonsillitis and progresses to a collection requiring drainage; can compromise the airway.
differential.trigger: Severe one-sided throat pain, trismus, muffled voice and uvular deviation

exam: Asymmetric swelling of the soft palate
Uvular deviation away from the affected side
imaging: CT neck with IV contrast showing a rim-enhancing peritonsillar fluid collection
Intraoral ultrasound showing a fluid collection

differential.name: Retropharyngeal abscess
differential.why_considered: A deep neck space infection that can cause airway obstruction and mediastinitis; more common in young children.
differential.trigger: Sore throat with neck stiffness, difficulty swallowing, fever and a toxic appearance, especially in a young child

history: Recent upper respiratory infection or pharyngitis
Neck stiffness or reluctance to move the neck
imaging: CT neck with IV contrast showing a rim-enhancing retropharyngeal fluid collection with fat stranding
Lateral neck x-ray showing widened retropharyngeal soft tissue space

differential.name: Acute bronchitis
differential.why_considered: Often follows a viral upper respiratory infection and can include sore throat, but the dominant symptom is cough.

history: Prominent cough lasting more than 5 days
Sore throat is mild and early
exam: Lung auscultation may show scattered wheezes or rhonchi
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal or shows only increased bronchovascular markings

differential.name: Influenza
differential.why_considered: Causes sore throat along with systemic symptoms and can be severe in high-risk groups.

history: Abrupt onset of high fever, chills and body aches
labs: Positive rapid influenza diagnostic test or molecular assay

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Can present with sore throat and fever, but lower respiratory symptoms and findings dominate.

imaging: Chest x-ray showing a focal infiltrate

differential.name: Sinusitis
differential.why_considered: Postnasal drip from sinusitis can cause sore throat, especially in the morning.

history: Symptoms lasting more than 10 days or worsening after initial improvement
imaging: CT sinuses showing mucosal thickening or air-fluid levels (not routine)

differential.name: Throat cancer (oropharyngeal or laryngeal)
differential.why_considered: A serious cause of persistent sore throat, especially with risk factors such as tobacco and alcohol use.
differential.trigger: Sore throat or hoarseness lasting more than 2–3 weeks, especially with weight loss, tobacco or alcohol use

history: Persistent sore throat or hoarseness for more than 2–3 weeks
exam: Mucosal lesion, ulcer or mass in the oral cavity, pharynx or larynx
labs: Biopsy of the lesion showing malignancy
imaging: CT or MRI of the neck showing a mass

severity.mild: Scratchy or raw throat, no fever or low-grade fever, able to eat and drink normally, no exudate or minimal erythema; self-limited viral illness
severity.moderate: Painful swallowing, fever up to about 101.5°F, visible pharyngeal erythema with or without exudate, tender cervical nodes; may be streptococcal and warrant testing
severity.severe: Severe pain limiting intake, high fever, marked exudate or asymmetric swelling, trismus, muffled voice, drooling or dehydration; consider deep neck infection or epiglottitis
severity.critical: Airway compromise with stridor, inability to swallow saliva, respiratory distress, tripod positioning or sepsis; requires immediate airway management

red_flags.finding: Drooling or inability to swallow saliva
red_flags.meaning: Suggests epiglottitis or another cause of impending airway obstruction; keep the patient calm and involve anesthesia or ENT immediately
Airway compromise; emergency evaluation and airway management

red_flags.finding: Uvular deviation or asymmetric soft palate swelling

red_flags.meaning: Suggests peritonsillar abscess or another deep neck infection

red_flags.finding: High fever over 102°F with toxic appearance
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a serious bacterial infection or systemic illness

red_flags.finding: Sore throat or hoarseness lasting more than 2–3 weeks
red_flags.meaning: Requires evaluation for malignancy, especially with tobacco or alcohol use

red_flags.finding: Dehydration or inability to keep fluids down
red_flags.meaning: May need IV fluids and pain control

complications.name: Acute rheumatic fever
clues: Rash or chorea weeks after the sore throat

special_populations.differences: Young children may not complain of sore throat and instead present with fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting or abdominal pain. Streptococcal pharyngitis is most common in ages 5–15; back up a negative rapid antigen test with a throat culture.
May have milder symptoms and lower fever but higher risk of dehydration and serious infections such as epiglottitis; sore throat may be the only sign of a serious problem.
Higher risk of severe or unusual infections such as Candida or herpes, and may lack classic inflammatory signs; symptoms can be prolonged and atypical.

Usually viral and self-limited; group A streptococcal infection can be more severe and should be treated promptly. Avoid unnecessary antibiotics and check pregnancy status before imaging or treatment decisions.

key_questions.question: When did the sore throat start, and how quickly did it come on?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset over hours to a day suggests group A streptococcal pharyngitis; gradual onset over 1–2 days with cold symptoms suggests a viral cause; rapid worsening over hours with severe pain suggests epiglottitis or a deep neck infection

key_questions.question: Is there a cough or runny nose along with the sore throat?
key_questions.looking_for: Prominent cough, runny nose, sneezing or hoarseness points to a viral cause and argues against streptococcal pharyngitis

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, and how high?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever at the onset supports streptococcal pharyngitis; high fever over 102°F with a toxic appearance raises concern for a serious bacterial infection

key_questions.question: Can you swallow your own saliva, or are you drooling?
key_questions.looking_for: Drooling or inability to swallow saliva suggests epiglottitis or impending airway obstruction and requires immediate evaluation

key_questions.question: Has your voice changed or become muffled?
key_questions.looking_for: A muffled 'hot potato' voice suggests peritonsillar abscess or epiglottitis

key_questions.question: Can you open your mouth fully, or does it hurt to open it?
key_questions.looking_for: Trismus suggests peritonsillar or parapharyngeal infection

key_questions.question: Is the pain worse on one side?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe one-sided pain suggests peritonsillar abscess or another deep neck infection

key_questions.question: Do you have any trouble breathing or noisy breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Stridor or respiratory distress indicates airway compromise and is an emergency

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any rash, joint pains or swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: A scarlatiniform rash suggests scarlet fever; migratory joint pains or swelling weeks later suggests acute rheumatic fever

key_questions.question: How long has this lasted, and has it been getting better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Most viral and streptococcal sore throats improve within 3–7 days; symptoms lasting more than 2–3 weeks, especially with hoarseness, require evaluation for malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you been around anyone with a sore throat or strep throat?
key_questions.looking_for: Close contact with someone who has strep throat supports group A streptococcal pharyngitis

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, vape or use alcohol heavily?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco and heavy alcohol use are risk factors for throat cancer, especially with persistent symptoms

key_questions.question: Have you had your tonsils out, or do you have a history of recurrent sore throats?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior tonsillectomy or recurrent streptococcal infections informs risk and management

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medications, including inhaled steroids or immunosuppressants?
key_questions.looking_for: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause oral candidiasis; immunosuppressants increase risk of severe or unusual infections

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status before antibiotics or imaging in anyone who could be pregnant

key_questions.question: Have you had any new sexual partners or unprotected oral sex?
key_questions.looking_for: Consider gonococcal pharyngitis in the appropriate exposure history

reasoning_points: Sore throat is most often viral and self-limited; the main task is to identify the minority who need testing or treatment for group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
Clinical features that suggest streptococcal pharyngitis include sudden onset, fever at the start, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymph nodes and absence of cough.
Prominent cough, runny nose, hoarseness or oral ulcers point to a viral cause and argue against testing or treating for group A streptococcus.
Use a rapid antigen detection test for group A streptococcus when clinical features suggest it; back it up with a throat culture in children and adolescents if the rapid test is negative.
Red flags such as drooling, muffled voice, trismus, severe one-sided pain, stridor or respiratory distress suggest epiglottitis or a deep neck infection and require urgent airway evaluation.

Consider infectious mononucleosis when there is marked posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, prolonged fatigue or atypical lymphocytes; avoid amoxicillin or ampicillin because of the rash risk.
Sore throat or hoarseness lasting more than 2–3 weeks, especially with tobacco or alcohol use, weight loss or a neck lump, requires evaluation for malignancy.
Check pregnancy status before antibiotics or imaging in anyone who could be pregnant.
